M22-P1-HL-1(a): Compare the two structures feature by feature: number of firms, entry, type of product and information. Define both terms first.
Draw a firm diagram for each. Then compare how much control each firm has over price, what happens to profit in the long run, and whether P = MC.
M22-P1-HL-1(b): Use the monopoly or collusive oligopoly model and define market power. Think about price, output and efficiency compared with a competitive market.
Draw the monopoly diagram and show the welfare loss. Then weigh it against what large firms can do that small ones cannot, on costs and innovation, using real firms.
M22-P1-HL-2(a): Split supply-side policies into market-based and interventionist ones. Define international competitiveness as well as competition.
Take one or two policies and show how each changes rivalry between domestic firms. Then use an AD/AS diagram to link productivity to the price level and export prices.
M22-P1-HL-2(b): Define interventionist supply-side policies and name the types of unemployment. Which type does each policy actually target?
Show the policy on an AD/AS diagram, then weigh it against demand-side and market-based options, cost and time lags. Use real countries as examples.
M22-P1-HL-3(a): Start with a PPC or opportunity cost example of comparative advantage, then question the assumptions the model rests on.
Go through the assumptions one by one (costs, factor mobility, technology, trade barriers). Then ask what specializing means for a poorer country's long-term structure.
M22-P1-HL-3(b): Define trading bloc and know the types, from free trade area to common market. Think about trade creation and trade diversion.
Explain the gains for members with a diagram, then the costs, including for non-members and national policy freedom. Use a real bloc such as the EU or ASEAN.
M22-P1-SL-1(a): You need two separate policies with two different goals. Think about the tools: subsidies, price controls, taxes and trade protection.
For each policy, draw its diagram and trace who gains: producers for the first, lower-income groups for the second. Explaining only one caps your mark.
M22-P1-SL-1(b): Use a demand and supply diagram with an indirect tax. List the stakeholders: consumers, producers, workers, government and society.
Show the tax burden on your diagram, then judge how PED and PES change who pays, and whether the tax corrects an externality. Use a real taxed good.
M22-P1-SL-2(a): Split supply-side policies into market-based and interventionist ones. Define international competitiveness as well as competition.
Take one or two policies and show how each changes rivalry between domestic firms. Then use an AD/AS diagram to link productivity to the price level and export prices.
M22-P1-SL-2(b): Define interventionist supply-side policies and name the types of unemployment. Which type does each policy actually target?
Show the policy on an AD/AS diagram, then weigh it against demand-side and market-based options, cost and time lags. Use real countries as examples.
M22-P1-SL-3(a): Keep growth (more output) and development (better lives) apart. Think about how a country is governed and how people are treated in society.
Pick two or three barriers. For each, trace the chain to investment or productivity, then to growth and to development separately. A PPC or poverty cycle can help.
M22-P1-SL-3(b): Define economic barriers, growth and development. Think about money, skills, infrastructure, debt and what the country relies on producing.
Explain how a few barriers hold back output and living standards, then judge how significant each is compared with political or social barriers. Use named countries.
M22-P2-HL-1(a)(i): It is about borrowing that has already happened. Think about what a borrower owes each period.
Say what exactly is being paid, and who the borrower could be.
M22-P2-HL-1(a)(ii): It is a single number linked to the Lorenz curve. What does it summarise about a country?
Add what its range of values tells you, or how it is built from areas on the Lorenz diagram.
M22-P2-HL-1(b)(i): Better access to Japan's market changes the buyers, not the farmers' costs. Which curve moves?
Label P and Q, draw both curves, and mark revenue as the P × Q rectangle before and after the shift.
M22-P2-HL-1(b)(ii): Balance of trade in goods = exports of goods − imports of goods. Use the Vietnam–Japan figures in Table 1.
Work out the balance for 2015 and for 2019 separately, then subtract the earlier from the later. Give units (US$ million).
M22-P2-HL-1(c): Economies of scale lower long-run average cost as output grows. Think about what a big farm can buy, borrow or use that a small one cannot.
Pick two distinct types. For each, say what a large farm can do and explain why it cuts the cost per unit.
M22-P2-HL-1(d): Comparative advantage is about lower opportunity cost, not producing more. Draw a PPC for each country with seafood and machinery on the axes.
Use the slopes to work out what each country gives up to make one more unit of each good. The one that gives up less should export that good.
M22-P2-HL-1(e): Use a money market diagram: vertical money supply, downward-sloping money demand, interest rate on the vertical axis.
Ask what a lower reserve requirement lets banks do with their deposits, and so what happens to the money supply. Then read off the new interest rate.
M22-P2-HL-1(f): Draw the exchange rate diagram for the dong. Reserve assets are the foreign currencies the central bank holds.
Think about what the central bank buys when it spends its reserves, and which dong curve that affects. Show the rate being held up.
M22-P2-HL-1(g): Compare two routes to development: exports to Japan and FDI from Japan. Define economic development and FDI.
Explain the gains from each using the texts (earnings, jobs, technology). Then weigh the costs, short run against long run, and who actually benefits.
M22-P2-HL-2(a)(i): These are the 17 United Nations goals for 2030. Text D names several problems that the goals target.
Give each goal its short official title, not a description of a problem.
M22-P2-HL-2(a)(ii): It is a type of trade barrier. How is it different from a quota?
Say what kind of payment it is and what goods it is placed on.
M22-P2-HL-2(b)(i): Better skills change what the economy can produce. Which line on a PPC shows potential output?
Label both axes with named goods, draw the original curve and a second one, and label both. Capacity decides which way the new curve sits.
M22-P2-HL-2(b)(ii): Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ price deflator × 100. Use the 2019 figures in Table 3.
Check which row is nominal GDP and which is the deflator (2010 base). Give the answer to 2 decimal places with units.
M22-P2-HL-2(c): Draw the poverty cycle as a loop that starts and ends with low income. Where does education fit into it?
Trace what more schooling does to skills, then to productivity, then to earnings. Show where that breaks the loop.
M22-P2-HL-2(d): Government spending is a component of AD. Use an AD/AS diagram with the price level on the vertical axis.
Decide which way AD moves when spending is cut, then show the new price level and real output. Label both axes.
M22-P2-HL-2(e): The current account records money flowing in and out. Which curves in the kwacha market do exports and imports affect?
A smaller deficit comes from more exports or fewer imports. Decide how each changes demand for or supply of kwacha, then mark the new rate.
M22-P2-HL-2(f): Draw a maximum price below equilibrium and shade the welfare loss triangle it creates.
Add a second, higher ceiling that is still below equilibrium. Compare the quantity traded and the size of the triangle at each ceiling.
M22-P2-HL-2(g): Separate growth from development. The texts mention aid, human capital, microfinance, infrastructure and fiscal policy.
Explain how each policy is meant to work with a diagram (poverty cycle, PPC or AD/AS). Then weigh cost, debt, time lags and who benefits, using Malawi's data.
M22-P2-SL-1(a)(i): It is investment across borders. How is it different from buying shares for a short-term return?
Say who invests, in what kind of asset, and where. Mention how long-term or controlling the stake is.
M22-P2-SL-1(a)(ii): It is a ratio. Think about who counts as part of the labour force.
Say what goes on top and what goes on the bottom, and how it is expressed.
M22-P2-SL-1(b)(i): Inflation rate = (CPI this year − CPI last year) ÷ CPI last year × 100. Use Table 1.
Do this for 2017, 2018 and 2019, each against the year before. Round to 2 decimal places and include %.
M22-P2-SL-1(b)(ii): Disinflation is not the same as falling prices. Think about what is actually falling.
Line up your three rates from (b)(i) in order and find where the rate first drops compared with the year before.
M22-P2-SL-1(b)(iii): Balance of trade = export revenue − import expenditure. Both figures are in Text A, paragraph 4.
Subtract in that order and keep the sign, since it tells you surplus or deficit. Include US$ billion.
M22-P2-SL-1(c): Full employment output is shown by the LRAS curve. Use Text B, paragraph 2 to see what the policies change.
Ask what the policies do to the economy's resources or how productive they are. Show the LRAS move and mark potential output before and after.
M22-P2-SL-1(d): Burning coal creates costs for people outside the market. Use an externalities diagram with MPC, MSC and MPB = MSB.
Compare the quantity the market produces with the quantity society would choose. Shade the welfare loss between them.
M22-P2-SL-1(e): Use the exchange rate diagram for the denar against the euro. Central banks intervene by buying or selling currency.
To stop the denar rising, decide whether the bank should buy or sell denar and which curve that shifts. Mark the rate being held down.
M22-P2-SL-1(f): Use an international trade diagram with domestic demand, domestic supply and a world price. A quota caps imports.
Show the price and imports with the quota first, then without it. Read off domestic production at each price.
M22-P2-SL-1(g): Know what a common market adds beyond a free trade area. Think about trade creation, FDI and factor movement.
Explain the gains with a diagram, then weigh the costs: competition for local firms, repatriated profits, loss of policy control. Use Texts A–C.
M22-P2-SL-2(a)(i): It measures output. Think about which goods count and where they are produced.
Say what is being added up, how it is valued, where, and over what period.
M22-P2-SL-2(a)(ii): The IHDI uses the same dimensions as the HDI, adjusted for inequality.
Name the dimensions as broad areas of life, not the specific indicators used to measure them.
M22-P2-SL-2(b)(i): Current account = trade balance + net income + net current transfers. Use Table 3.
Find the balance for 2017 and for 2018 separately, watching the sign on each row. Then subtract 2017 from 2018 and give units.
M22-P2-SL-2(b)(ii): Growth rate = (real GDP this year − real GDP last year) ÷ last year × 100. Use Table 3.
Use 2017 as the base. Round to 2 decimal places and add %.
M22-P2-SL-2(c): Foreigners need leone to pay for Sierra Leone's exports. Which curve in the leone market is that?
Decide how lower export revenue moves that curve, then mark the new exchange rate. Label the axes as price and quantity of leone.
M22-P2-SL-2(d): Fuel is a cost of production for most firms. Which AD/AS curve does a cost change move?
Decide the direction of that shift, then show what happens to the average price level and real output. Label both axes.
M22-P2-SL-2(e): Draw the poverty cycle loop from low income back to low income. Free schooling removes a cost for households.
Ask what families do with money no longer spent on fees, and what schooling does to future earnings. Show where the loop breaks.
M22-P2-SL-2(f): Modern farming changes how efficiently rice is produced. Which curve does that affect?
Decide the direction of the shift, then show the new equilibrium price and quantity. Label P and Q.
M22-P2-SL-2(g): Separate growth from development. Look for interventions in the texts: subsidy changes, education, health care and NGOs.
Explain each intervention with a diagram, then weigh cost, funding, inflation, and whether benefits reach the poor. Use the text data.
M22-P3-HL-1(a)(i): Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100. Use Table 1.
The labour force is the employed plus the unemployed, not the whole population. Add those first, then divide.
M22-P3-HL-1(a)(ii): Think about how the prices and output of farm products behave from year to year, and what that means for farmers' incomes.
Explain why those incomes are unpredictable, then ask what that does to a family's ability to plan and spend for the future.
M22-P3-HL-1(a)(iii): PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Use the domestic demand curve Dd in Figure 1.
Read Qd at US$1500 and at US$1800, then find each % change from the starting values. Keep quantity on top.
M22-P3-HL-1(a)(iv): At a world price, exports = domestic supply − domestic demand. Export value = exports × price.
Read Sd and Dd at both prices in Figure 1, find exports and their value at each, then subtract. Watch the units on the quantity axis.
M22-P3-HL-1(a)(v): Compare it with regressive and proportional taxes. The key is how the tax changes as income rises.
Talk about the share of income paid, not just the amount.
M22-P3-HL-1(a)(vi): The price paid already includes VAT, so the VAT is not simply the rate times that price.
First find the price before VAT by dividing by (1 + the VAT rate), then apply the rate to that. Include the currency.
M22-P3-HL-1(a)(vii): Think long run: a lower corporate tax affects firms' incentive to invest. Which curve shows potential output?
Label the axes (price level, real GDP), draw the LRAS before and after, and mark potential output on each.
M22-P3-HL-1(a)(viii): Look at Table 3 for gaps between women and men, for example in schooling, health or work.
Pick two gaps. For each, trace how it affects productivity, income or family wellbeing, and so development.
M22-P3-HL-1(b): Pick one policy, such as a tax, transfer or spending change. Define income inequality and consider a Lorenz curve.
Explain how it works with a diagram and Burundi's data, then weigh cost, funding, time lags and side effects before recommending it.
M22-P3-HL-2(a)(i): Each driver ignores the costs they impose on others. Use an externalities diagram for consumption with MPB, MSB and MSC.
Show where drivers choose to be and where society would want them. Shade the welfare loss and use costs from the text.
M22-P3-HL-2(a)(ii): The S + t curve includes the taxes. Table 4 shows how much of the price is tax.
Add up the tax parts per litre in Table 4. The vertical gap between the two supply curves should equal that total at every quantity. Label the new curve.
M22-P3-HL-2(a)(iii): Tax revenue = tax per unit × quantity sold. Use Figure 2.
Take the tax per litre from (a)(ii) and the quantity at the equilibrium with tax. Watch the units on the quantity axis.
M22-P3-HL-2(a)(iv): Consumer surplus lost is the area between the price with tax and the price without it, to the left of demand.
Read both prices and both quantities from Figure 2. The area is a trapezium: price gap × average of the two quantities.
M22-P3-HL-2(a)(v): PES = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price. Use the no-tax supply curve you drew.
Pick two points on that curve, find both % changes and compare the result with 1. You can also note which axis the line meets.
M22-P3-HL-2(a)(vi): Profit per litre is one of the price components in Table 4. Total profit = profit per unit × quantity.
Find the profit or margin row in Table 4 and multiply by the daily quantity in Figure 2. Include units.
M22-P3-HL-2(a)(vii): It is an assumption of standard economic theory about how consumers make decisions.
Say what consumers are assumed to try to get the most of, and how they weigh their options.
M22-P3-HL-2(a)(viii): Behavioural economics lists ways real people fall short of rational choice, such as limited information, biases and habits.
Pick one limitation, explain it, then show how it keeps New Delhi commuters driving when other options could suit them better.
M22-P3-HL-2(b): Choose one policy that tackles the external cost of driving, such as a tax, a charge, public transport or a nudge.
Explain it with an externalities diagram and the text data, then weigh cost, effectiveness, fairness and time lags before recommending it.
N22-P1-HL-1(a): Use the positive consumption externality diagram. Key terms: marginal private benefit, marginal social benefit, allocative efficiency, welfare loss.
Explain why buyers only consider their own benefits, show the market and socially optimal quantities, shade the welfare loss, and give a real example.
N22-P1-HL-1(b): Asymmetric information means one side of a deal knows more. Think about adverse selection, moral hazard, and the policies that target them.
Explain how the information gap causes market failure, then weigh each policy on cost, enforcement and side effects, using real examples such as insurance or used cars.
N22-P1-HL-2(a): Think about what happens when debt grows faster than the economy. Define government debt and budget deficit.
Explain the links from high debt to interest payments, opportunity cost, credit ratings and future taxes, and how these affect other macro objectives. Use real examples.
N22-P1-HL-2(b): Use the short-run and long-run Phillips curves. Define inflation, unemployment and the natural rate of unemployment.
Explain the short-run trade-off with a diagram, then weigh expectations, the long-run view and supply shocks, using real episodes such as the 1970s or 2021 to 2023.
N22-P1-HL-3(a): Both are stages of economic integration. Define each one clearly.
Compare them point by point on what can move freely between members and how each treats non-member countries. Give a real example of each.
N22-P1-HL-3(b): Think about trade creation, trade diversion, economies of scale and loss of policy independence.
Explain the gains with a diagram, then weigh the costs for different stakeholders and in the short vs long run. Brexit is a useful example.
N22-P1-SL-1(a): Choose two ways governments intervene in markets and define each one.
For each, draw a demand and supply diagram, explain the change in price and quantity, say why a government would use it, and give an example.
N22-P1-SL-1(b): Key ideas: non-rivalry, non-excludability and the free-rider problem.
Explain why markets under-provide these goods, then weigh government provision against cost, opportunity cost and private alternatives. Use examples such as street lighting.
N22-P1-SL-2(a): Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation. Think about which macroeconomic objectives it can target.
Pick two goals, and for each explain the mechanism with an AD/AS diagram or other theory, using a real example.
N22-P1-SL-2(b): Use AD/AS with a recessionary gap and the Keynesian multiplier. Define fiscal policy and recessionary gap.
Show expansionary fiscal policy on a diagram, then weigh time lags, debt, crowding out and the size of the multiplier, using real examples such as 2008 or 2020.
N22-P1-SL-3(a): Use a floating exchange rate diagram. A change in the value of a currency starts with a change in demand for it or supply of it.
For each factor, decide which side of the currency market it affects, show the shift on a labelled diagram, and give a real example.
N22-P1-SL-3(b): Think about how appreciation changes export and import prices, and what that means for AD, inflation, growth and the current account.
Explain the effects with diagrams, then weigh stakeholders such as exporters, importers and consumers, price elasticities, and short vs long run. Use real examples.
N22-P2-HL-1(a)(i): Demand is more than simply wanting a product. Think about the conditions economists attach to it.
Say what the buyer must be besides interested, and add the two conditions that any quantity demanded is measured under.
N22-P2-HL-1(a)(ii): Contrast it with a linear economy where goods are made, used and thrown away.
Say what happens to products and materials after use, and include two separate features for full marks.
N22-P2-HL-1(b)(i): YED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income. Text A, paragraph 2 gives one of these.
Use Table 1's income for 2008 and 2018 to find the percentage change in income, then divide the demand change by it.
N22-P2-HL-1(b)(ii): Compare Tanzania's Gini coefficients for 2008 and 2018 in Table 2. A Lorenz curve diagram shows inequality.
Decide whether the Gini rose or fell, then draw two Lorenz curves whose gap from the equality line matches. Label both axes and each curve.
N22-P2-HL-1(c): Crowding out happens when government borrowing competes with private borrowing. Think about what that does to interest rates.
Trace the chain from interest rates to investment and consumption, then to AD, and show it on a labelled AD/AS diagram with the price level.
N22-P2-HL-1(d): Use the international trade diagram with domestic supply, domestic demand and the world price. A subsidy affects producers' costs.
Decide how the subsidy changes domestic supply, shift that curve, and show the new domestic output and imports at the world price. Label everything.
N22-P2-HL-1(e): Foreign firms investing in Tanzania must pay in shillings. Which side of the shilling market does that affect?
Shift that curve on a shilling exchange rate diagram, label the axes and curves, and show the new exchange rate.
N22-P2-HL-1(f): Think about harm to third parties and the environment from the pipeline in Text C. Is this a production or a consumption externality?
Draw the private and social cost curves with demand, compare the market quantity with the social optimum, and shade and label the welfare loss.
N22-P2-HL-1(g): Keep growth (real GDP) separate from development (living standards). Key terms: barriers, poverty, inequality, informal sector.
Use evidence from Texts A to C on farming, skills, investment and inequality with a diagram, then weigh which barriers matter most and whether growth helps development.
N22-P2-HL-2(a)(i): It is one type of foreign aid. Contrast it with development aid.
Say when this aid is given and what form it usually takes.
N22-P2-HL-2(a)(ii): This is a market structure. Contrast it with perfect competition.
Say how many firms there are, and add one feature that protects that position.
N22-P2-HL-2(b)(i): GNI = GDP + net income from abroad.
Take GDP and the income flows in and out from Table 3, find the net figure first, then add it to GDP. Include units.
N22-P2-HL-2(b)(ii): An indirect tax is paid to the government by producers. Which curve does a change in firms' costs affect?
Decide whether the tax raises or lowers costs per unit, shift that curve to match, and label P, Q, both curves and both equilibria.
N22-P2-HL-2(c): A PPC shows what an economy can produce with its resources. What kind of resource were the damaged buildings?
Decide whether Lebanon now has more or fewer factors of production, move the whole curve to match, and label both axes with two goods.
N22-P2-HL-2(d): Remittances are income households receive from abroad. Which components of AD might they pay for?
Decide how a fall affects that spending, shift the right curve on a labelled AD/AS diagram, and show the new real output.
N22-P2-HL-2(e): Text D, paragraph 3 describes Lebanon's current account. Think about what imports and exports do in the market for pounds.
Paying for imports means swapping pounds for foreign currency; foreigners buying exports need pounds. Shift the matching curve(s) and mark the new exchange rate.
N22-P2-HL-2(f): Use the monopoly diagram with AR, MR, MC and AC. Profit or loss depends on comparing AR and AC at the chosen output.
Find output where MR = MC, read the price from AR, compare it with AC there and shade the area. Use Text E, paragraph 2 to explain why.
N22-P2-HL-2(g): Read Text F, paragraph 1 and group each condition as demand-side, supply-side or institutional. Keep growth and development separate.
Explain each condition's effect with an AD/AS diagram, using Texts D to F, then weigh short-run costs against long-run gains, effects on the poor, and governance problems.
N22-P2-SL-1(a)(i): Say what the benchmark is and who sets it.
N22-P2-SL-1(a)(ii): Contrast it with the formal economy that the government tracks.
Include two separate ways this activity escapes the government's view or control.
N22-P2-SL-1(b)(i): Unemployment rate = number unemployed ÷ labour force × 100.
Take the unemployed figure and the labour force for 2019 from Table 1, check they are in the same units, then divide and convert to a percentage.
N22-P2-SL-1(b)(ii): Convert the taka price into dollars using the 2019 exchange rate in Table 1.
Check how Table 1 states the rate (taka per dollar or dollars per taka) and divide or multiply to match. Round to cents.
N22-P2-SL-1(b)(iii): Compare the exchange rate in 2010 and 2019 in Table 1, or the shirt's dollar price in both years.
If the same taka price now buys a different number of dollars, what has happened to the taka's value? Decide from that.
N22-P2-SL-1(c): Use a demand and supply diagram for Bangladeshi garments. Revenue is price × quantity.
Shift the curve that Text A, paragraph 5 describes, then show the revenue rectangle before and after. Label P, Q, curves and both equilibria.
N22-P2-SL-1(d): Use a tariff diagram for the US market. Bangladeshi producers' revenue is shown by the imports on that diagram.
Show the world price with and without the 15 % tariff, compare import quantities before and after, and shade what Bangladeshi producers receive. Label all curves.
N22-P2-SL-1(e): Check how imports changed in Table 1. Importers must swap taka for foreign currency: which side of the taka market is that?
Shift the matching curve on a taka exchange rate diagram, label the axes and curves, and explain what happens to the equilibrium rate.
N22-P2-SL-1(f): Look at the Gini coefficient in Table 2 for 2010 and 2019. A Lorenz curve shows how income is shared.
Decide whether inequality rose or fell, then draw two curves placed to match relative to the line of equality. Label axes and explain the change.
N22-P2-SL-1(g): Break the goal into parts: sustained growth, inclusion, productive employment and decent work. Consider export-led growth and the informal economy.
Use evidence from the texts on women's jobs, wages, safety and trade with a diagram, then weigh risks such as reliance on one export, working conditions and skills.
N22-P2-SL-2(a)(i): It relates to the government's budget in a single year. Contrast it with national debt.
Name the two sides of the government budget and say how they compare.
N22-P2-SL-2(a)(ii): Which account does it belong to, and how is it different from FDI?
Name the kind of assets that are bought and why the investor buys them.
N22-P2-SL-2(b)(i): YED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income. Text E and Table 3 give what you need.
Find the percentage change in health care demand and in income for 2010 to 2018 using (new − old) / old, then divide. Give two decimal places.
N22-P2-SL-2(b)(ii): The current account covers trade in goods and services, income and current transfers. Find those rows in Table 6.
Combine only the current account items, adding inflows and subtracting outflows. Leave out financial account items such as portfolio investment. Include units.
N22-P2-SL-2(c): Who else gains when someone receives health care? Choose the externality diagram that shows that.
Draw the private and social benefit curves with supply, mark the market and socially optimal quantities, and shade the welfare loss a subsidy would remove.
N22-P2-SL-2(d): A drought disrupts production, for example of crops. Is that a demand-side or a supply-side shock?
Shift the matching curve on an AD/AS diagram labelled with price level and real GDP, and show what happens to real output.
N22-P2-SL-2(e): Use the international trade diagram with domestic supply, domestic demand and the world price. A quota limits the quantity of imports.
Show the quota as a fixed import gap, find the new domestic price where it fits, then explain what happens to consumers' price, quantity and surplus.
N22-P2-SL-2(f): The central bank holds foreign currency reserves. How can it use them in the market for pesos?
Think about what the bank buys when it spends reserves, shift the matching curve on a labelled peso diagram, and show the effect on the rate.
N22-P2-SL-2(g): Separate fiscal from monetary policy, and growth from development. Key terms: redistribution, budget deficit, inflation targeting.
Use Text D evidence on tax rates, social spending, deficit rules, the inflation target and infrastructure with a diagram, then weigh conflicts between objectives and who benefits.
N22-P3-HL-1(a)(i): Use AC = TC ÷ Q and MC = change in TC ÷ change in Q to fill the gaps in Table 1.
Work row by row: where AC is given, multiply by Q to get TC; where TC is known, divide by Q or subtract the previous row's TC.
N22-P3-HL-1(a)(ii): In long-run monopolistic competition, firms earn only normal profit. Your diagram needs AR, MR, MC and AC.
Find output where MR = MC, then think about where AC must be relative to AR at that output if profit is normal. Label axes, curves and output.
N22-P3-HL-1(a)(iii): Consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price. The price floor changes both the price consumers pay and the quantity they buy.
Read price and quantity before and after the floor in Figure 1, find each triangle with ½ × base × height, subtract, and state the direction and units.
N22-P3-HL-1(a)(iv): Recall the condition for allocative efficiency and check whether it holds at the free market equilibrium in Figure 1.
Then find the quantity produced under the price floor, read the price and the supply curve's height at that quantity, and compare them.
N22-P3-HL-1(a)(v): The expenditure figure already includes the 6.5 % tax. You need the amount before tax first.
Divide the total spending by (1 + tax rate) to get the pre-tax amount, then subtract that from the total spending. Include units.
N22-P3-HL-1(a)(vi): PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Table 3 gives the PED for business travel.
Rearrange so % change in quantity = PED × % change in price, use the business PED, and state the direction with a percentage sign.
N22-P3-HL-1(a)(vii): The relevant measure here is income elasticity of demand. Compare the values for domestic and international routes in Table 3.
A higher YED means demand responds more to income changes. Use the 3 % income rise to compare the two routes, or calculate both.
